name: Semicolons
sub: Joining two full sentences
rule: A semicolon ( ; ) joins two complete sentences.
trick: Cover one side. Can each side stand alone as a sentence? If both can, a semicolon works.

examples.text: I studied all week; the test felt easy.
Because I studied all week; the test felt easy.
examples.note: "Because I studied all week" can't stand alone.

another.text: A semicolon is a period wearing a hat. Anywhere a period could go, a semicolon can go instead. If a period would look wrong in that spot, so would a semicolon.
another.example:
I was hungry. I made toast.
I was hungry; I made toast.

questions.blank: The bus was late__ we walked to school.
questions.why: "The bus was late" and "we walked to school" are both full sentences. A comma alone can't join two sentences.

questions.blank: After the game__ we got pizza.
questions.why: "After the game" can't stand alone, so a semicolon doesn't work there.

questions.blank: My phone died__ I couldn't text you back.
questions.why: Both sides are full sentences. A period would work, so a semicolon works.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Running late; she grabbed her keys.
She was running late; she grabbed her keys.
questions.why: "Running late" isn't a full sentence. "She was running late" is.

questions.blank: Coach blew the whistle__ practice was over.
questions.why: Two full sentences. Cover either side and the other still stands alone.

name: Colons
sub: Lists and explanations
rule: A colon ( : ) comes after a complete sentence and points to what's next: a list, an example, or an explanation.
trick: Read only the words before the colon. Are they a full sentence? If not, no colon.

examples.text: I need three things: eggs, milk, and bread.
I need: eggs, milk, and bread.
examples.note: "I need" isn't a full sentence.

another.text: A colon is a drumroll. First you say a whole thing. Then the colon goes "ta-da!" and shows what you were talking about.
another.example: I want one thing for my birthday: a puppy.

questions.blank: She had one goal__ win the state title.
questions.why: "Win the state title" isn't a full sentence, so no semicolon. The colon points to what her goal was.

questions.blank: We packed__ snacks, water, and sunscreen.
questions.why: "We packed" isn't a full sentence. Let the list follow the verb with no punctuation.

questions.blank: The answer was simple__ practice every day.
questions.why: The first part is a full sentence, and the second part explains it. That's a colon's job.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: My favorite subjects are: math and art.
I have two favorite subjects: math and art.
questions.why: "My favorite subjects are" isn't finished. "I have two favorite subjects" is.

questions.blank: He brought everything he needed__ a pencil, a calculator, and his ID.
questions.why: A full sentence, then a list of what he brought. Colon.

name: Its or it's
sub: The most common apostrophe trap
rule: it's means "it is" or "it has." its means "belongs to it."
trick: Swap in "it is." If the sentence still makes sense, use it's. If not, use its.

examples.text: It's cold out. The dog wagged its tail.
The dog wagged it's tail.
examples.note: "The dog wagged it is tail" makes no sense.

another.text: It's is two words squished together: it is. The little mark is where the i from "is" fell out. If you can't un-squish it back into "it is," don't use the mark.
another.example:
It's raining. → It is raining. ✓
The dog wagged it's tail. → The dog wagged it is tail? ✗ Use its.

questions.blank: __ going to rain later.
questions.why: "It is going to rain later" works, so it's.

questions.blank: The team lost __ first game.
questions.why: "Lost it is first game" doesn't work. The game belongs to the team, so its.

questions.blank: __ been a long week.
questions.why: It's can also mean "it has." "It has been a long week."

questions.blank: The phone fell and __ screen cracked.
questions.why: The screen belongs to the phone. "It is screen" makes no sense.

questions.blank: I think __ your turn.
questions.why: "I think it is your turn" works, so it's.

name: Subject and verb
sub: is or are, has or have
rule: The verb has to match its subject. One thing: is, was, has. More than one: are, were, have.
trick: Cross out the words between the subject and the verb, like "of the cookies." Then read it again.

examples.text: The box of cookies is empty.
examples.note: Cross out "of cookies": The box is empty.

examples.text: The box of cookies are empty.
examples.note: The box is one thing.

another.text: Find who or what the sentence is really about. Then cover everything between that word and the verb with your finger. Now listen to whether it sounds right.
another.example:
The box of crayons (is / are) on the floor.
Cover "of crayons": The box is on the floor. ✓

questions.blank: The list of chores __ long.
questions.why: Cross out "of chores": The list is long. One list.

questions.blank: My friends from camp __ visiting.
questions.why: Cross out "from camp": My friends are visiting. More than one friend.

questions.blank: Each of the players __ a jersey.
questions.why: "Each" means one at a time. Cross out "of the players": Each has a jersey.

questions.blank: The keys on the table __ mine.
questions.why: Cross out "on the table": The keys are mine.

questions.blank: The noise from the trucks __ loud.
questions.why: Cross out "from the trucks": The noise was loud. It's the noise, not the trucks.

name: Commas around extra info
sub: Interrupters and names
rule: Extra information that could be lifted out of the sentence gets a comma on both sides.
trick: Lift the phrase out. If the sentence still works without it, wrap it in two commas. One comma is never enough.

examples.text: My brother, who is twelve, plays drums.
examples.note: Lift out "who is twelve": My brother plays drums.

examples.text: My brother, who is twelve plays drums.
examples.note: Only one comma. The second one is missing.

another.text: The extra part is like a sticker on a sentence. Two commas hold the sticker on. You can peel it off, and the sentence underneath is still a whole sentence.
another.example:
My brother, who is seven, loves dinosaurs.
Peel off the sticker: My brother loves dinosaurs.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: The movie, which came out in May, was a hit.
The movie, which came out in May was a hit.
questions.why: "Which came out in May" is extra info. It needs a comma on both sides.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
questions.why: "My cousin" can be lifted out: Maya is visiting. Two commas.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: The park, however, closes at dusk.
The park however, closes at dusk.
questions.why: "However" interrupts the sentence, so it gets a comma on each side.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Students, who skip breakfast, do worse on tests.
Students who skip breakfast do worse on tests.
questions.why: "Who skip breakfast" isn't extra here. Lift it out and the sentence says all students do worse. No commas.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: The new phone, released last week, sold out.
The new phone released last week, sold out.
questions.why: "Released last week" can be lifted out: The new phone sold out. Two commas.

name: Who is doing the action?
sub: Dangling modifiers
rule: A describing phrase at the start of a sentence has to describe the very next thing after the comma.
trick: Read the opening phrase, then ask "who did that?" That person or thing must come right after the comma.

examples.text: Running to the bus, Jamal dropped his bag.
examples.note: Who was running? Jamal. He comes right after the comma.

examples.text: Running to the bus, the bag fell.
examples.note: The bag wasn't running.

another.text: Read the sentence like a cartoon. Whoever comes right after the comma is doing the first part. If the cartoon is silly, the wrong person is after the comma.
another.example:
Running to the bus, my backpack fell open.
Cartoon: a backpack running to the bus. Silly!
Fix: Running to the bus, I let my backpack fall open.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Walking home, the rain soaked Priya.
Walking home, Priya got soaked by the rain.
questions.why: Who was walking home? Priya, so she comes right after the comma.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: After finishing the test, the pencils were put away by the students.
After finishing the test, the students put away their pencils.
questions.why: Who finished the test? The students. Pencils don't finish tests.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Exhausted from practice, the couch looked perfect to Leo.
Exhausted from practice, Leo collapsed on the couch.
questions.why: Who was exhausted? Leo, not the couch.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Built in 1920, the house still has its original windows.
Built in 1920, the owners love the house's original windows.
questions.why: What was built in 1920? The house. The owners weren't built.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Hoping for a snow day, the forecast was checked every hour.
Hoping for a snow day, we checked the forecast every hour.
questions.why: Who was hoping? We were. A forecast can't hope.

name: Comma splices
sub: A comma can't join two sentences by itself
rule: Two complete sentences can't be joined with only a comma. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or so.
trick: If you could put a period there, a comma alone is wrong.

examples.text: It was raining, so we stayed in.
It was raining, we stayed in.
examples.note: Two full sentences held together by a comma. That's a splice.

another.text: A comma is like tape. It can hold on a little word, but it can't hold two whole sentences together by itself. For that you need glue: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus "and," "but," or "so."
another.example:
I was tired, I went to bed. ✗ (tape)
I was tired, so I went to bed. ✓ (glue)
I was tired. I went to bed. ✓ (glue)

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: The store was closed, we went home.
The store was closed, so we went home.
questions.why: Both halves are full sentences. The comma needs a helper word like so.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: I love this song; I play it every day.
I love this song, I play it every day.
questions.why: Two full sentences. A semicolon can hold them; a comma alone can't.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: She practiced for months, she still felt nervous.
She practiced for months, but she still felt nervous.
questions.why: Comma plus but joins two sentences correctly. Comma alone is a splice.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
questions.why: "Dinner is ready" and "come eat" are both full sentences. A period fixes the splice.

questions.stem: Which one is correct?
options: Hoping to win, the team practiced late.
The team practiced late, they hoped to win.
questions.why: The second option joins two full sentences with only a comma. The first opens with a describing phrase, which is fine.

name: Apostrophes
sub: Owning something vs more than one
rule: An apostrophe shows owning (the dog's bowl). Plain plurals never get one (two dogs).
trick: Ask: does something belong to it? Yes: apostrophe. Is it just more than one? No apostrophe.

examples.text: The girl's bike. The girls' bikes. Three girls.
I have two dog's.
examples.note: Nothing belongs to the dogs. Just two dogs.

another.text: The apostrophe is a little flag that says "this belongs to someone." Plant the flag right after the owner's name. One kid owns it: kid's. Lots of kids own it: kids'. If nobody owns anything, no flag.
another.example:
the kid's hat (one kid owns it)
the kids' hats (many kids own them)
three kids (nobody owns anything, no flag)

questions.blank: The __ tail is fluffy.
questions.why: The tail belongs to the cat. Apostrophe.

questions.blank: We saw three __ at the park.
questions.why: Just more than one dog. Nothing belongs to them. No apostrophe.

questions.blank: Both __ lockers were open.
questions.why: More than one student, and the lockers belong to them. Apostrophe after the s.

questions.blank: __ car is in the shop.
questions.why: The car belongs to Marcus. One owner, so apostrophe then s.

questions.blank: The __ are selling tickets.
questions.why: More than one senior, nothing owned. No apostrophe.

name: Transition words
sub: However, therefore, for example
rule: A transition word tells the reader how the next sentence connects to the last one: a contrast, a result, or an example.
trick: Read the sentence before and the sentence after. Do they disagree (however), does one cause the other (therefore), or is the second an example (for example)?

examples.text: It rained all day. However, the game went on.
examples.note: Disagree: rain vs game went on.

examples.text: It rained all day. Therefore, the game was canceled.
examples.note: Cause: rain led to canceled.

another.text: Transition words are road signs. "But" and "however" mean turn around, the next thing is the opposite. "So" and "therefore" mean keep going, this happened because of that. "Also" and "for example" mean more of the same.
another.example:
It rained. ___ we stayed inside.
Same direction, because of the rain → So we stayed inside.

questions.blank: The trail was steep. __, we reached the top before noon.
questions.why: Steep trail vs reaching the top early. They pull in different directions, so a contrast word.

questions.blank: He forgot his lunch. __, he was hungry all afternoon.
questions.why: Forgetting lunch caused the hunger. Result word.

questions.blank: Many animals hibernate. __, bears sleep most of the winter.
questions.why: Bears are an example of animals that hibernate.

questions.blank: The library is quiet. __, it has fast wifi.
questions.why: Both are good things about the library. Adding, not contrasting.

questions.blank: The recipe looked easy. __, it took three hours.
questions.why: Looked easy vs took three hours. Contrast.

name: Slope and starting value
sub: What the numbers in y = mx + b mean
rule: In y = mx + b, m is the slope: how much y changes each step. b is the start: the value of y when x is 0.
trick: The number attached to x is the slope. The number by itself is the start.

examples.note: Slope 3, starts at 5.

examples.text: Cost = 40 + 12m
examples.note: $40 to start, then $12 more each month.

another.text: Think of a piggy bank. You start with some money. Every week you drop in the same amount. The money you started with is b. The amount each week is the slope, because it's how fast the bank grows.
another.example:
Start with $40. Add $12 every week.
After w weeks: 12w + 40

questions.stem: What is the slope of y = 4x − 7?
questions.why: 4 is attached to x, so it's the slope.

questions.stem: Where does y = 2x + 9 start (the y-intercept)?
questions.why: 9 is the number by itself. When x is 0, y is 9.

questions.stem: A gym costs C = 25 + 10m dollars for m months. What does 25 mean?
questions.why: 25 is the number by itself, so it's the start: what you pay before any months.

questions.stem: Same gym: C = 25 + 10m. What does 10 mean?
questions.why: 10 is attached to m (months), so it's how much the cost goes up each month.

questions.stem: Which line is steeper?
questions.why: Steeper means a bigger slope. 5 is bigger than 2. The 8 only moves where the line starts.

name: Solving for x
sub: Undo what was done to x
rule: To solve for x, undo each operation in reverse order. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
trick: Undo adding with subtracting, undo multiplying with dividing. Clear the loose number first, then the number stuck to x.

examples.note: Subtract 4: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.
Add 6: x = 16.

another.text: x is a present wrapped in layers. 3x + 4 means someone wrapped x in "times 3," then in "plus 4." Unwrap the outside layer first: take away the 4. Then take off the 3. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other side too.
another.example:
2x + 5 = 11
Take the +5 off both sides → 2x = 6
Take the ×2 off both sides → x = 3

questions.stem: x + 8 = 15. What is x?
questions.why: Undo the +8 by subtracting 8 from both sides: x = 7.

questions.stem: 4x = 28. What is x?
questions.why: Undo the ×4 by dividing both sides by 4: x = 7.

questions.stem: 2x + 3 = 11. What is x?
questions.why: Subtract 3: 2x = 8. Divide by 2: x = 4.

questions.stem: 5x − 10 = 20. What is x?
questions.why: Add 10: 5x = 30. Divide by 5: x = 6.

questions.stem: x/3 = 9. What is x?
questions.why: Undo the ÷3 by multiplying both sides by 3: x = 27.

name: What a system's solution is
sub: Two equations, one answer that fits both
rule: The solution to a system is the one (x, y) pair that makes both equations true at the same time. On a graph, it's where the two lines cross.
trick: To check an answer, plug the x and y into both equations. If either one fails, it's not the solution.

examples.text: x + y = 7 and x − y = 1
examples.note: Try (4, 3): 4 + 3 = 7 ✓ and 4 − 3 = 1 ✓. Solution.

examples.text: Try (5, 2) for the same system
examples.note: 5 + 2 = 7 ✓ but 5 − 2 = 3 ✗. Not the solution.

another.text: Draw two straight roads on paper. Where do they cross? Usually in exactly one spot. That spot is the answer. If the roads never touch, there's no answer. If they're the same road, every spot works.
another.example:
Two roads cross once → one answer
Two roads side by side forever → no answer
One road drawn twice → every point is an answer

questions.stem: Which pair solves x + y = 10 and x − y = 4?
questions.why: 7 + 3 = 10 ✓ and 7 − 3 = 4 ✓. (5, 5) and (6, 4) pass the first equation but fail the second.

questions.stem: Two lines cross at (2, 5). What is the solution to that system?
questions.why: The crossing point is the solution. The first number is x, the second is y.

questions.stem: Two lines are parallel and never touch. How many solutions does the system have?
questions.why: No crossing point means no (x, y) pair works for both. No solution.

questions.stem: Is (3, 1) a solution to y = x − 2 and x + y = 4?
options: No, it fails the first equation
No, it fails the second equation
questions.why: y = 3 − 2 = 1 ✓ and 3 + 1 = 4 ✓. Both work.

questions.stem: Is (1, 4) a solution to y = 2x + 2 and y = x + 2?
questions.why: First: 2(1) + 2 = 4 ✓. Second: 1 + 2 = 3, not 4 ✗. It has to pass both.

name: Inequalities
sub: Reading the sign, and when it flips
rule: Solve an inequality like an equation. One extra rule: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, flip the sign.
trick: The open side of the sign faces the bigger thing. x > 3 means x is bigger than 3. Flip only on a negative multiply or divide.

examples.note: Subtracting 2 doesn't flip anything.
Divided by −2, so the sign flipped.

another.text: Picture a seesaw with one side up high. Multiplying by a negative flips the whole seesaw over, so the high side becomes the low side. That's why the > sign has to flip too.
another.example:
−x > 3
Multiply both sides by −1 and flip: x < −3
Check: x = −4 → −(−4) = 4, and 4 > 3 ✓

questions.stem: Which number makes x > 4 true?
questions.why: x has to be bigger than 4. 4 itself doesn't count, since the sign isn't ≥.

questions.stem: Solve x − 3 ≤ 2.
questions.why: Add 3 to both sides. No negative multiply or divide, so the sign stays.

questions.stem: Solve −3x < 12.
questions.why: Divide by −3 and flip the sign: x > −4. Check x = 0: −3(0) = 0 < 12 ✓.

questions.stem: Solve 2x + 1 > 7.
questions.why: Subtract 1: 2x > 6. Divide by positive 2: x > 3. No flip.

questions.stem: A ride requires h ≥ 48 inches. Who can ride?
questions.why: ≥ means 48 or more. Exactly 48 counts.

name: Percents
sub: Percent of, percent off, percent up
rule: Percent means "out of 100." To find a percent of a number, turn the percent into a decimal and multiply.
trick: Move the decimal two places left: 30% → 0.30. Then multiply.

examples.text: Price goes up 10%
examples.note: Multiply by 1.10

another.text: Percent means "out of 100 pieces." Pretend the number is a pizza cut into 100 tiny slices. 25% is 25 of those slices. 10% is the easy one: move the decimal point one spot left. Build the rest from that.
another.example:
10% of 80 = 8
20% = two of those = 16
5% = half of one = 4

questions.stem: What is 10% of 80?
questions.why: Move the decimal one spot left: 80 → 8.

questions.stem: What is 25% of 40?
questions.why: 0.25 × 40 = 10. Or: 25% is a quarter, and a quarter of 40 is 10.

questions.stem: Shoes cost $60 and are 50% off. What's the sale price?
questions.why: 50% is half. Half of $60 is $30 off, so you pay $30.

questions.stem: A $20 shirt goes up 10%. What's the new price?
12 out of 50 students walk to school. What percent is that?
questions.why: Out of 50 is half of out of 100. Double both: 24 out of 100, so 24%.

name: Ratios and rates
sub: Scaling a recipe up or down
rule: A ratio compares two amounts. If one amount gets multiplied, the other gets multiplied by the same number.
trick: Find what you multiplied the known number by. Multiply the other number by the same thing.

examples.text: 2 cups flour for 3 eggs. How much flour for 9 eggs?
examples.note: 3 → 9 is ×3, so 2 → 6 cups.

examples.text: 60 miles in 1 hour. How far in 4 hours?
examples.note: 1 → 4 is ×4, so 60 → 240 miles.

another.text: Find out what one costs, or what one does. Then multiply. If 4 cookies cost $2, one cookie costs 50 cents. Want 10 cookies? 10 times 50 cents.
another.example:
4 cookies → $2
1 cookie → $0.50
10 cookies → $5

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 apples for 2 pies. How many apples for 6 pies?
questions.why: 2 → 6 pies is ×3. So 3 → 9 apples.

questions.stem: A car goes 150 miles on 5 gallons. How far on 1 gallon?
questions.why: 150 ÷ 5 = 30 miles per gallon.

questions.stem: 5 pencils cost $2. How much do 20 pencils cost?
The ratio of cats to dogs at a shelter is 3 to 4. There are 12 dogs. How many cats?
questions.why: 4 → 12 dogs is ×3. So 3 → 9 cats.

questions.stem: A printer prints 40 pages in 2 minutes. How long for 100 pages?
questions.why: 40 pages in 2 minutes is 20 pages a minute. 100 ÷ 20 = 5 minutes.

name: Unit conversion
sub: Minutes to hours, feet to inches
rule: To change units, multiply or divide by the conversion number. Going to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger. Going to a bigger unit, the number gets smaller.
trick: Ask: should I end up with more or fewer? Inches are smaller than feet, so 3 feet becomes more inches (36), not fewer.

examples.text: 3 feet to inches
examples.note: Smaller unit, more of them: 3 × 12 = 36 inches.

examples.text: 180 minutes to hours
examples.note: Bigger unit, fewer of them: 180 ÷ 60 = 3 hours.

another.text: Think about how many of the small thing fit in the big thing. 60 minutes fit in 1 hour. Going from hours to minutes, you end up with more pieces, so multiply. Going from minutes to hours, you end up with fewer pieces, so divide.
another.example:
2 hours → minutes: 2 × 60 = 120 minutes
180 minutes → hours: 180 ÷ 60 = 3 hours

questions.stem: How many minutes are in 2 hours?
questions.why: Minutes are smaller, so more of them: 2 × 60 = 120.

questions.stem: How many feet are in 48 inches?
questions.why: Feet are bigger, so fewer of them: 48 ÷ 12 = 4.

questions.stem: A snack has 1.5 kilograms of nuts. How many grams is that?
questions.why: 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500 grams.

questions.stem: A movie runs 150 minutes. How long is that in hours?
A room is 4 yards long. How many feet is that?
questions.why: 1 yard is 3 feet. 4 × 3 = 12 feet.

name: Mean and median
sub: Two kinds of average
rule: Mean: add everything up and divide by how many. Median: put the numbers in order and take the middle one.
trick: Median always starts with sorting. With an even count, the median is halfway between the two middle numbers.

examples.note: Mean: 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Median: sort to 3, 5, 7, middle is 5.
Mean: 116 ÷ 4 = 29. Median: between 4 and 10 = 7.

another.text: Mean is "share it out evenly." Five kids pool their candy and split it equally; what each kid gets is the mean. Median is "line up and pick the middle kid." One kid with a giant bag changes the sharing a lot but doesn't change who's in the middle.
another.example:
Candies: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 → mean 4, median 4
Swap the 6 for 100 → mean 22.8, median still 4

questions.stem: What is the mean of 4, 8, and 12?
What is the median of 9, 2, 7?
questions.why: Sort first: 2, 7, 9. The middle number is 7.

questions.stem: What is the median of 1, 3, 5, 11?
questions.why: Even count. The two middle numbers are 3 and 5, and halfway between them is 4.

questions.stem: Five friends have test scores of 90, 92, 94, 96, and 98. One more friend scores 20. Which changes more?
questions.why: The 20 drags the mean from 94 down to about 81.7. The median only moves from 94 to 93.

questions.stem: A team's scores are 10, 10, 10, 10, 50. What is the median?
questions.why: Already sorted. The middle (third) number is 10. The mean would be 18, but that's not the median.

name: Pythagorean theorem
sub: Finding the missing side of a right triangle
rule: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c². The two short sides are a and b. The longest side, across from the right angle, is c.
trick: c is always the longest side and is always alone on one side of the equation. Square, add, square root.

examples.text: Legs 3 and 4. Longest side?
Longest side 13, one leg 5. Other leg?

another.text: Draw a square on each side of a right triangle. The two small squares together have exactly as much room as the big square. That's all a² + b² = c² says.
another.example:
Short sides 3 and 4: squares of 9 and 16, together 25.
The big square is 25, so the long side is 5.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. How long is the longest side?
A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. How long is the longest side?
The longest side is 10 and one leg is 6. How long is the other leg?
questions.why: 36 + b² = 100, so b² = 64 and b = 8. The longest side goes alone.

questions.stem: A ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 3 feet from the wall and it reaches 4 feet up. How long is the ladder?
questions.why: The ladder is the longest side. 9 + 16 = 25, √25 = 5.

questions.stem: Which side is c in a² + b² = c²?
options: The side across from the right angle
questions.why: c is always the longest side, the one across from the right angle.

name: Angles in a triangle
sub: They always add to 180
rule: The three angles inside any triangle add up to 180°. A straight line is also 180°.
trick: Add the two angles you know, then subtract from 180.

examples.text: Angles 60° and 70°. Third angle?
Right triangle with a 30° angle

another.text: Cut a paper triangle into its three corners. Push the corners together, points touching. They always make a perfectly straight line. A straight line is 180°, so the three corners always add up to 180°.
another.example:
Two corners are 60° and 70°.
60 + 70 = 130, so the last corner is 180 − 130 = 50°.

questions.stem: A triangle has angles of 50° and 60°. What is the third angle?
A right triangle has one angle of 35°. What is the other non-right angle?
An equilateral triangle has all equal angles. Each one is:
Two angles of a triangle are each 40°. What is the third?
Two angles sit next to each other on a straight line. One is 110°. What is the other?
questions.why: A straight line is 180. 180 − 110 = 70.

name: Reading a table
sub: Find a value, spot a trend
rule: Find the row, find the column, read where they meet. Then read down a column: do the numbers go up, go down, or both?
trick: Most ACT Science answers are sitting in the table. You almost never need to know the science.

examples.text: At 60 °C, how much sugar dissolved?
examples.note: Row 60, column Sugar → 290 g

another.text: A table is like a seating chart. Rows are the people, columns are what we know about them. Put one finger on the row and one finger on the column, then slide them together. Where the fingers meet is your number.
another.example:
Row: Tuesday. Column: Rain.
Fingers meet at 2 inches. That's Tuesday's rain.

questions.stem: At 40 °C, how much sugar dissolved?
questions.why: Row 40, slide across to Sugar: 240 g.

questions.stem: As the water gets hotter, the sugar dissolved:
questions.why: Read down the column: 200, 240, 290, 360. It goes up every time.

questions.stem: Which temperature dissolved 290 g?
questions.why: Find 290 in the Sugar column, then look left: 60 °C.

questions.stem: Predict: at 100 °C, the sugar dissolved would most likely be:
questions.why: The trend goes up as temperature goes up, so past 80 °C it should keep going past 360 g.

questions.stem: Between which two temperatures did the sugar dissolved increase the most?
questions.why: 20 to 40 added 40 g. 60 to 80 added 70 g. The biggest jump is at the bottom of the table.

name: Trends and in-between values
sub: Interpolate and extrapolate
rule: If a value sits between two rows, the answer sits between their results. If it's past the last row, follow the pattern onward.
trick: Between two rows: pick a number between the two results. Past the table: keep going in the same direction.

examples.text: Height at 15 minutes?
examples.note: Between 10 and 20 min, so between 6 and 8 cm. About 7.

examples.text: Height at 40 minutes?
examples.note: Goes up 2 every 10 min, so 12 cm.

another.text: If a plant is 4 inches tall on Monday and 6 inches on Wednesday, it was probably about 5 inches on Tuesday. Nobody measured it, but it had to pass 5 to get there. Tables work the same way: in-between times get in-between numbers.
another.example:
Monday 4 in., Wednesday 6 in. → Tuesday about 5 in.
Friday? Keep growing 1 inch a day → about 8 in.

questions.stem: What was the plant's height at 25 minutes?
questions.why: 25 is between 20 and 30, so the height is between 8 and 10. About 9.

questions.stem: If the pattern continues, what will the height be at 50 minutes?
questions.why: It adds 2 cm every 10 minutes. 30 → 40 → 50 min is 10 → 12 → 14 cm.

questions.stem: How much does the plant grow every 10 minutes?
questions.why: 4, 6, 8, 10: each step is +2 cm.

questions.stem: At what time was the plant about 7 cm tall?
questions.why: 7 is between 6 (at 10 min) and 8 (at 20 min), so about 15 minutes.

questions.stem: As time increases, plant height:
questions.why: Read down the height column: it goes up at every step.

name: Variables
sub: What was changed, what was measured
rule: The independent variable is what the scientist changes on purpose. The dependent variable is what they measure. Everything else stays the same.
trick: Changed = independent. Measured = dependent. In a table, the first column is usually what was changed.

examples.text: Change the light, measure plant height
examples.note: Light is independent. Height is dependent.

another.text: Think of a cookie experiment. You decide how long to bake each batch. That's the independent variable, because you picked it. Then you see how brown the cookies get. That's the dependent variable, because it depends on what you picked.
another.example:
You picked: 8, 10, or 12 minutes
You watched: how brown they got

questions.stem: A student gives plants different amounts of light and measures how tall they grow. What was changed on purpose?
questions.why: The student chose the light amounts before starting. That's the independent variable.

questions.stem: Same experiment. What was measured?
questions.why: Height is what the student waited to find out. That's the dependent variable.

questions.stem: To make it a fair test, what should stay the same for every plant?
questions.why: Only the light should change. If water changed too, you couldn't tell which one made the plants grow.

questions.stem: In this table, what was changed on purpose?
questions.why: Temperature is in the first column, set in neat steps of 20. Sugar dissolved is what got measured.

questions.stem: A scientist drops balls from different heights and times how long they take to land. The dependent variable is:
questions.why: Time is what the scientist measured. Height is what they changed.

name: Controls
sub: The one group nothing happens to
rule: A control is the group that gets no treatment. You compare every other group to it to see if the treatment did anything.
trick: Look for the group with zero, none, or plain water. That's the control.

examples.text: Testing a fertilizer: Group A gets 0 g, B gets 5 g, C gets 10 g
examples.note: Group A (0 g) is the control.

examples.text: Testing a medicine
examples.note: The group that gets a sugar pill is the control.

another.text: Say you give your plant magic juice and it grows. Was it the juice, or would it have grown anyway? The control is a second plant that gets plain water. If both plants grow the same, the juice did nothing.
another.example:
Plain-water plant grew 3 cm. Magic-juice plant grew 3 cm.
The juice did nothing.

questions.stem: Students test whether salt makes water boil faster. Which pot is the control?
options: The pot with 1 spoon of salt
The pot with 2 spoons of salt
questions.why: The control gets no treatment: plain water, no salt.

questions.stem: Why does an experiment need a control?
options: To see what happens with no treatment
To make the experiment take longer
questions.why: The control shows what would happen anyway, so you can tell if the treatment made a difference.

questions.stem: In a medicine trial, one group gets a pill with no medicine in it. That group is:
questions.why: No medicine means no treatment. That's the control.

questions.stem: Plants with fertilizer grew 5 cm. The control grew 5 cm too. What does this show?
questions.why: Same growth with and without fertilizer means the fertilizer didn't do anything.

questions.stem: A scientist tests three different fertilizers but forgets to grow a plant with none. What's the problem?
options: There's nothing to compare the fertilizers against
questions.why: Without a no-fertilizer plant, you can't tell how much growth was from the fertilizer and how much would have happened anyway.
